task.label: In Text · p. 551 · question 1
task.sourceText: 2   Explain why there is a limit to  how large a cell can grow.
task.reviewStatus: Original wording retained; geometric crop plus complete source context.

tasks.firstResponse: As a cell enlarges, volume and metabolic demand rise faster than membrane surface area. Eventually the membrane cannot exchange enough nutrients and wastes for the larger volume. Growth of the organism therefore requires additional cells.
tasks.visibleSupport: pp.550–551: surface-area/volume explanation and cube model.
tasks.limitationsOrAlternatives: This is outside the narrow L03–04 teaching; complete source context supplies it.

task.label: In Text · p. 551 · question 3
task.sourceText: 2   Brieﬂ y summarize how advances  in technology led to the new  theories about the origin of cells.
task.reviewStatus: Original wording retained; geometric crop plus complete source context.

tasks.firstResponse: Improved microscope lenses let scientists resolve cells and observe their division. Synthetic stains then made chromatin and individual chromosomes visible, allowing the sequence of cell division to be described. These observations supported new cells arising from existing cells rather than spontaneous generation.
tasks.visibleSupport: pp.550–551: improved lens technology, Virchow account, dyes and Flemming.
tasks.limitationsOrAlternatives: This is source-assisted historical content, not taught by L03–04.

task.label: In Text · p. 552 · question 5
task.sourceText: 2   In what structures is the genetic  information of a cell contained?  Where are these structures located?
task.reviewStatus: Original wording retained; geometric crop plus complete source context.

tasks.firstResponse: Genetic information is carried by DNA in chromosomes; in the eukaryotic nuclear-genome context here, these chromosomes are in the nucleus.
tasks.visibleSupport: p.551 genetic-information explanation and p.552 Figure 16.2.
tasks.limitationsOrAlternatives: The question is framed by eukaryotic nuclear DNA; do not generalize to all DNA being nuclear in every kind of cell.

task.label: In Text · p. 552 · question 6
task.sourceText: 2   What is a centromere and where  would you ﬁ nd it?
task.reviewStatus: Original wording retained; geometric crop plus complete source context.

tasks.firstResponse: A centromere is the specialized chromosome region seen as a constriction on the condensed chromosome; in a replicated chromosome it is associated with the joined sister chromatids and their spindle attachment region.
tasks.visibleSupport: pp.551–552, chromosome figure; L03 definition and actual diagram.
tasks.limitationsOrAlternatives: It need not lie at the geometric centre, and is not an entire chromosome or homologue pair.

task.label: In Text · p. 552 · question 10
task.sourceText: 2   Write a sentence that clearly  differentiates these terms:  diploid, haploid, polyploid.
task.reviewStatus: Original wording retained; geometric crop plus complete source context.

tasks.firstResponse: Haploid cells have one chromosome set (n), diploid cells two sets (2n), and polyploid cells more than two complete sets, such as 3n or 4n.
tasks.visibleSupport: p.552 chromosome-number text.
tasks.limitationsOrAlternatives: Unreplicated versus replicated is different from ploidy; matched physical pairing is not required to be diploid.

task.label: In Text · p. 553 · question 11
task.sourceText: 2   What is a karyotype?
task.reviewStatus: Original wording retained; geometric crop plus complete source context.

tasks.firstResponse: A karyotype is the chromosome complement of an individual, commonly represented as an ordered image of chromosomes arranged in matched pairs by size, centromere position and banding pattern.
tasks.visibleSupport: p.553 explanation and actual Figure 16.4.
tasks.limitationsOrAlternatives: Both the complement and its organized display are acceptable in this source context.

task.label: In Text · p. 555 · question 14
task.sourceText: 2   Brieﬂ y describe each phase.
task.reviewStatus: Original wording retained; geometric crop plus complete source context.

firstResponse.G1: The cell grows and performs ordinary metabolic functions.
firstResponse.S: DNA is replicated so each chromosome has two sister chromatids.
firstResponse.G2: Further growth, energy rebuilding and manufacture of division structures prepare the cell for division.
firstResponse.Mitosis: The nuclear genetic material is distributed into two separate matching chromosome sets.
firstResponse.Cytokinesis: Cytoplasm and organelles are partitioned to form two daughter cells.

tasks.visibleSupport: Full p.555 shows Q13 asks main phases of the cell cycle; pp.553–555 identify G1, S, G2, mitosis, cytokinesis.
tasks.limitationsOrAlternatives: The isolated crop “each phase” is underspecified; the complete page resolves the antecedent. Do not answer only PMAT.

task.label: In Text · p. 556 · question 15
task.sourceText: 2   Name the three important  functions of mitosis and  cytokinesis.
task.reviewStatus: Original wording retained; geometric crop plus complete source context.

tasks.firstResponse: Growth of the organism; maintenance by replacing worn-out or dead cells; repair of damaged tissue.
tasks.visibleSupport: p.556 three explicit function bullets.
tasks.limitationsOrAlternatives: Source-assisted; these are not all developed in narrow L04.

task.label: In Text · p. 556 · question 16
task.sourceText: 2   Why must each daughter cell have  the correct genetic information?
task.reviewStatus: Original wording retained; geometric crop plus complete source context.

tasks.firstResponse: Each daughter needs the genetic instructions required to produce its molecules and carry out its normal functions. Correct replication and distribution preserve the necessary chromosome complement so new cells can support growth, maintenance and repair.
tasks.visibleSupport: p.556 function and required-event paragraphs; p.551 genetic information determines structure/function.
tasks.limitationsOrAlternatives: A complete complement is necessary; normal division is not an absolute guarantee against mutation.

task.label: In Text · p. 558 · question 17
task.sourceText: 2   What are the four phases of  mitosis?
task.reviewStatus: Original wording retained; geometric crop plus complete source context.

tasks.visibleSupport: pp.557–558 four-stage headings and figure; L04 PMAT.
tasks.limitationsOrAlternatives: Interphase is part of cell cycle, not one of the four mitotic phases.

task.label: In Text · p. 558 · question 18
task.sourceText: 2   List the key events that happen  to chromosomes in each phase.
task.reviewStatus: Original wording retained; geometric crop plus complete source context.

firstResponse.Prophase: Already-replicated chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes.
firstResponse.Metaphase: Replicated chromosomes align individually at the cell equator with the sisters oriented toward opposite poles.
firstResponse.Anaphase: Sister chromatids separate; each is now a chromosome, and the copies move toward opposite poles.
firstResponse.Telophase: The separated chromosome groups reach opposite poles and decondense as new nuclear envelopes form.

tasks.visibleSupport: pp.557–558 descriptions and actual Figure 16.8; L04 teaching.
tasks.limitationsOrAlternatives: Source calls separated copies chromatids in places; use individual chromosomes after separation consistently.

task.label: Section 16 1 · p. 555 · question 1
task.sourceText:
1. Give two reasons that cell division is necessary for 
a plant to grow from a seedling into a tree.
task.reviewStatus: Original wording retained; geometric crop plus complete source context.

firstResponse.reason1: The tree requires more cells as its tissues increase in size; individual cells cannot grow without limit because membrane exchange capacity is limited relative to volume.
firstResponse.reason2: During growth, cell division also replaces worn-out or damaged cells, maintaining functioning tissues as the tree develops.

tasks.visibleSupport: p.550 size limit and replacement; p.556 growth, maintenance and repair.
tasks.limitationsOrAlternatives: Also accept two clearly distinguished aspects of the need for new cells: increasing cell number and keeping individual cells small enough for exchange. Prompt does not specify one unique pair of reasons.

task.label: Section 16 1 · p. 555 · question 7
task.sourceText:
7. Suppose that you are examining a human cell with 
22 pairs of autosomes, one X chromosome, and one 
Y chromosome. Did this cell come from a male or a 
female? Is the cell somatic or a gamete? Diploid or 
haploid? Explain.
task.reviewStatus: Original wording retained; geometric crop plus complete source context.

firstResponse.given: 22 pairs of autosomes plus one X and one Y chromosome = 44+2=46 chromosomes.
firstResponse.sex: In the textbook’s typical human chromosomal model, male (XY).
firstResponse.cellType: Somatic, rather than a normal gamete, because there are chromosome pairs and two sex chromosomes.

tasks.visibleSupport: pp.552–555 typical human chromosome counts and XX/XY model.
tasks.limitationsOrAlternatives: XY does not establish every aspect of sex/phenotype in all biological cases. The question’s male/female model is a simplification; chromosome number alone does not prove cell identity without its normal-model assumptions.

task.label: Section 16 2 · p. 561 · question 4
task.sourceText: 4. What role does the spindle apparatus play in cell division?
task.reviewStatus: Original wording retained; geometric crop plus complete source context.

tasks.firstResponse: The spindle apparatus organizes chromosome positioning and distribution. Microtubules attach at chromosome kinetochore/centromere regions, align replicated chromosomes, and help move separated sister copies toward opposite poles so each daughter nucleus gets a complete complement.
tasks.visibleSupport: p.558 spindle/microtubule and metaphase/anaphase descriptions; L04.
tasks.limitationsOrAlternatives: Not every spindle microtubule attaches directly to a chromosome; the apparatus also separates poles.

tasks.firstResponse: Cell-cycle signals normally regulate when cells start, continue and stop division. If regulation is disrupted, cells may divide uncontrollably and give rise to cancer; accumulation of those abnormal cells can form a tumour.

task.label: Section 16 2 · p. 561 · question 6
task.sourceText:

 6. The scientists in a lab have isolated a substance that 
prevents cells from synthesizing microtubules. What 
impact would this substance have on cell division? Explain.
task.reviewStatus: Original wording retained; geometric crop plus complete source context.

tasks.firstResponse: Blocking microtubule synthesis prevents a functional mitotic spindle from forming normally. Chromosomes cannot be positioned and segregated accurately, so division may arrest or produce abnormal chromosome distributions rather than two normal daughter nuclei.
tasks.visibleSupport: p.558 spindle fibres are protein microtubules and guide chromosome movement; L04 spindle mechanism.
tasks.limitationsOrAlternatives: The given is prevention of microtubule synthesis, not inhibition of DNA copying. Outcome need not be a single guaranteed abnormal distribution because arrest is also possible.

task.sourceText:

 7. A scientist studying a group of somatic cells notices that 
upon the completion of the cell cycle half of the daughter 
cells have no chromosomes and the other half have 
92 chromosomes. In what phase of mitosis did an 
error most likely occur? Explain your reasoning.
task.reviewStatus: Original wording retained; geometric crop plus complete source context.

firstResponse.given: After the cell cycle, half the daughter cells have 0 chromosomes and half have 92.
firstResponse.mostLikelyPhase: Anaphase, the stage responsible for segregation of separated sister copies.
firstResponse.reasoning: Failure to distribute the chromosomes to opposite poles could deliver all 92 separated chromosomes to one future daughter and none to the other. Under the usual human somatic model, 46 chromosomes replicated before mitosis provide those 92 separated copies.
firstResponse.limitation: The question does not explicitly name the species or original chromosome count. The final imbalance identifies failed segregation, but an earlier spindle-attachment error at metaphase could cause the later anaphase failure; counts alone cannot uniquely locate the initiating defect.

tasks.visibleSupport: p.561 exact given; p.558 anaphase mechanism; L03 boundary/counting explanation.
tasks.limitationsOrAlternatives: Do not silently replace 0/92 with 45/47 or assume single-chromosome nondisjunction. Accept a justified earlier spindle-attachment cause alongside the intended anaphase outcome.
